packet.headline_seed: Danes try to tow dead whale from island beach after failed German rescue
packet.description_seed: An environmental team want to move the whale from Anholt to the Danish mainland, but they have had to pause the operation.

what: Danes try to tow dead whale from island beach after failed German rescue

clean_source_blocks.text: Danish environment officials have begun an operation to move the carcass of a humpback whale from an island beach across the sea to mainland Denmark. The dead whale was discovered on the shores of Anholt island last weekend, two weeks after a private mission to save the humpback from being stranded on Germany's Baltic Sea coast ended in failure. Denmark's environmental protection agency said the carcass, not far from the beach, was causing significant disruption, and decided it should be transported by sea to the port of Grenaa, about 57km (35 miles) to the south-west. Islanders had earlier been urged to keep away from the whale because of the risk of infection. One woman on Anholt said before the operation to move it had begun: "It's around 20-30m (65-100ft) from the beach but it's drifting along the beach."
An environmental team want to move the whale from Anholt to the Danish mainland, but they have had to pause the operation.

The whale has gained in size in recent days because of a build-up of gas as the carcass decomposes, and there is widespread concern it might explode. "That's nature. I know some people are worried, but I'm not," the islander told the BBC. Early on Thursday, an emergency response team arrived off the coast of Anholt to begin the operation to move the whale, first by towing the carcass into deeper water and then transporting it with a larger boat to Grenaa. However, Jane Hansen from the environmental protection agency said that the operation had not been a success: "After several attempts, the whale has now become stranded on a sandbank some distance from the shore." "The operation has therefore been temporarily paused while the emergency response team explores alternative options for transporting the whale," she added.
Some German tourists have appeared on the island in recent days to follow developments about the whale that some media outlets labelled "Timmy" - named after the sandban ---

original_article.research:
[Lähde: BBC World]
Danish environment officials have begun an operation to move the carcass of a humpback whale from an island beach across the sea to mainland Denmark.

The dead whale was discovered on the shores of Anholt island last weekend, two weeks after a private mission to save the humpback from being stranded on Germany's Baltic Sea coast ended in failure.

Denmark's environmental protection agency said the carcass, not far from the beach, was causing significant disruption, and decided it should be transported by sea to the port of Grenaa, about 57km (35 miles) to the south-west.

Islanders had earlier been urged to keep away from the whale because of the risk of infection.

One woman on Anholt said before the operation to move it had begun: "It's around 20-30m (65-100ft) from the beach but it's drifting along the beach."

The whale has gained in size in recent days because of a build-up of gas as the carcass decomposes, and there is widespread concern it might explode.

"That's nature. I know some people are worried, but I'm not," the islander told the BBC.

Early on Thursday, an emergency response team arrived off the coast of Anholt to begin the operation to move the whale, first by towing the carcass into deeper water and then transporting it with a larger boat to Grenaa.

However, Jane Hansen from the environmental protection agency said that the operation had not been a success: "After several attempts, the whale has now become stranded on a sandbank some distance from the shore."

"The operation has therefore been temporarily paused while the emergency response team explores alternative options for transporting the whale," she added.

The agency said it still aimed to take the whale to the harbour at Grenaa for a post-mortem examination as well as to allow researchers to collect "valuable scientific samples".

However, the next attempt is unlikely to take place before the end of Denmark's long public holiday weekend.

Exactly how the whale ended up on an island off Denmark's East Jutland coast in the Kattegat strait is a mystery. The barge that carried the mammal away from Germany released it into the sea about 70km (45 miles) from the northern tip of Denmark.

The saga has transfixed Germans since early March, and has left islanders on Anholt bemused by the continued interest in the story.

Some German tourists have appeared on the island in recent days to follow developments about the whale that some media outlets labelled "Timmy" - named after the sandban

Danish environment officials have begun an operation to move the carcass of a humpback whale from an island beach across the sea to mainland Denmark.

The dead whale was discovered on the shores of Anholt island last weekend, two weeks after a private mission to save the humpback from being stranded on Germany's Baltic Sea coast ended in failure.

Denmark's environmental protection agency said the carcass, not far from the beach, was causing significant disruption, and decided it should be transported by sea to the port of Grenaa, about 57km (35 miles) to the south-west.

Islanders had earlier been urged to keep away from the whale because of the risk of infection.

One woman on Anholt said before the operation to move it had begun: "It's around 20-30m (65-100ft) from the beach but it's drifting along the beach."

The whale has gained in size in recent days because of a build-up of gas as the carcass decomposes, and there is widespread concern it might explode.

"That's nature. I know some people are worried, but I'm not," the islander told the BBC.

Early on Thursday, an emergency response team arrived off the coast of Anholt to begin the operation to move the whale, first by towing the carcass into deeper water and then transporting it with a larger boat to Grenaa.

However, Jane Hansen from the environmental protection agency said that the operation had not been a success: "After several attempts, the whale has now become stranded on a sandbank some distance from the shore."

"The operation has therefore been temporarily paused while the emergency response team explores alternative options for transporting the whale," she added.

The agency said it still aimed to take the whale to the harbour at Grenaa for a post-mortem examination as well as to allow researchers to collect "valuable scientific samples".

However, the next attempt is unlikely to take place before the end of Denmark's long public holiday weekend.

Exactly how the whale ended up on an island off Denmark's East Jutland coast in the Kattegat strait is a mystery. The barge that carried the mammal away from Germany released it into the sea about 70km (45 miles) from the northern tip of Denmark.

The saga has transfixed Germans since early March, and has left islanders on Anholt bemused by the continued interest in the story.

Some German tourists have appeared on the island in recent days to follow developments about the whale that some media outlets labelled "Timmy" - named after the sandban

payload.title: Kuolleen ryhävalaan siirto Tanskan Anholtin rannalta keskeytyi
payload.summary: Tanskan ympäristöviranomaiset yrittävät siirtää kuolleen ryhävalaan Anholtin saaren rannalta mantereelle, mutta operaatio on toistaiseksi keskeytetty valaan juututtua hiekkasärkälle.
payload.content:
Tanskan ympäristöviranomaiset ovat yrittäneet siirtää kuolleen ryhävalaan ruhon Anholtin saaren rannalta meriteitse Grenaan satamaan, mutta operaatio ei ole edennyt suunnitellusti. Valas on ollut lähellä rantaa ja aiheuttanut viranomaisten mukaan merkittävää häiriötä, minkä lisäksi saaren asukkaita on kehotettu pysymään loitolla tartuntariskin vuoksi.

## Ruho halutaan kuljettaa mantereelle

Kuollut ryhävalas löydettiin Anholtin rannalta viime viikonloppuna. Tanskan ympäristönsuojeluvirasto päätti, että ruho kuljetetaan meritse Grenaan satamaan, joka sijaitsee noin 57 kilometrin päässä saaresta lounaaseen.

Viranomaisten suunnitelmana oli ensin hinata ruho syvempään veteen ja siirtää se sen jälkeen suuremmalla aluksella mantereelle. Torstaina Anholtin edustalle saapui pelastus- ja valmiusryhmä aloittamaan siirtoa.

Operaatio osoittautui kuitenkin vaikeaksi. Ympäristönsuojeluviraston Jane Hansenin mukaan useiden yritysten jälkeen valas päätyi hiekkasärkälle jonkin matkan päähän rannasta. Tämän vuoksi siirto keskeytettiin väliaikaisesti, kun ryhmä selvittää muita vaihtoehtoja ruhon kuljettamiseksi pois alueelta.

## Hajoava ruho herättää huolta

Valas on kasvanut viime päivinä kooltaan, koska hajoamisessa syntyvä kaasu on kertynyt ruhon sisään. Tämän vuoksi on herännyt huolta siitä, että ruho voisi revetä tai räjähtää. Eräs Anholtin asukas kuvasi valaan olleen ennen siirtoyritystä noin 20–30 metrin päässä rannasta ja ajautuneen rantaviivan suuntaisesti.

Viranomaiset ovat kehottaneet ihmisiä pitämään etäisyyttä valaaseen mahdollisen infektiovaaran takia. Tapaus on herättänyt huomiota myös saaren ulkopuolella, ja Anholtille on saapunut saksalaisia matkailijoita seuraamaan tilanteen etenemistä.

Valas oli aiemmin yhteydessä Saksassa epäonnistuneeseen yksityiseen pelastusyritykseen. Se löydettiin Tanskasta noin kaksi viikkoa sen jälkeen, kun yritys pelastaa ryhävalas rantautumiselta Saksan Itämeren rannikolla oli päättynyt tuloksetta. Tanskan viranomaiset arvioivat nyt, miten ruho saadaan siirrettyä turvallisesti pois Anholtin rannan läheisyydestä.
summary_bullets: Tanskan viranomaiset yrittävät siirtää kuolleen ryhävalaan Anholtin saarelta Grenaan satamaan.
Operaatio keskeytettiin, kun valas juuttui hiekkasärkälle useiden siirtoyritysten jälkeen.
Saaren asukkaita on kehotettu pysymään loitolla ruhosta tartuntariskin vuoksi.
